definition: Taken by surprise; startled.
note: Old English onbæc meant 'to the back'. 'Taken aback' was first a sailing term, for a ship whose sails were suddenly pressed back against the mast.
hints: How a sudden surprise leaves you.

definition: To lower someone in rank or dignity.
note: From Old French, built from a Latin word for 'low'. To abase yourself is to make yourself small in front of someone.

definition: To become less intense; to die down.
note: From Old French abatre, 'to beat down'. Storms, fevers and anger all abate.
hints: What a storm does as it passes.

definition: A building where monks or nuns live and worship.
note: From Old French abaie, ultimately from the Aramaic abba, 'father', via the title of the man who ran it.

definition: The head of a monastery.
note: From Latin abbas, from Aramaic abba, 'father'. The monks' leader was, in name, their father.

definition: To hate something deeply.
note: From Latin abhorrere, 'to shrink back in horror', with the same root as horror.

definition: To put up with; to tolerate.
note: From Old English abidan, 'to wait'. 'Abode', a place you wait in, comes from the same word.
hints: To tolerate, or to obey a rule.

definition: A home; the place where someone lives.
note: Once meant the act of waiting. A place you stay in came to be named after the staying.
hints: A rather grand word for home.
Related to a word meaning to stay.

definition: To stop something before it is finished.
note: From Latin aboriri, 'to miscarry', from ab- 'away' and oriri 'to arise'. Missions and computer tasks are aborted too.

definition: Concerning; on the subject of.
note: Old English onbutan meant 'on the outside of'. Going around something became talking around it.
hints: What a story is said to be.
Also means roughly, as with numbers.

definition: Higher than; over.
note: From Old English abufan, 'on top'. 'Above board' comes from card players keeping their hands visible over the table.
hints: Where the sky is, from the ground.

definition: Cruel or improper treatment, or misuse.
note: From Latin abusus, 'used up' or 'misused'. It began as a word for wrong use before it meant cruelty.
hints: Power can be put to this.

definition: A seemingly bottomless chasm.
note: From Greek abussos, 'bottomless', from a- 'not' and bussos 'depth'.
hints: A drop with no visible floor.

definition: The nut of the oak tree.
note: From Old English æcern, originally any wild fruit. The spelling bent towards 'oak' and 'corn' later.
hints: Great oaks are said to grow from it.

definition: Sharp and bitter in smell or taste.
note: From Latin acer, 'sharp'. It was shaped to look like 'acid' by people who assumed the two were related.
hints: It catches the back of your throat.

definition: Someone who performs a role on stage or screen.
note: From Latin, 'a doer', from agere 'to do'. In law it once meant the person who brings a case.

definition: Severe and sudden; or sharp.
note: From Latin acutus, 'sharpened'. An acute angle is a sharp one, and an acute illness strikes quickly.
hints: Describes an angle under ninety degrees.

definition: An old saying held to be true.
note: From Latin adagium, a proverb. 'A stitch in time' is one.
hints: Old wisdom in a short sentence.

definition: To change to suit new conditions.
note: From Latin adaptare, 'to fit to'. Darwin's species and novels turned into films both do it.
hints: A book may be this for the screen.

definition: Very skilled at something.
note: From Latin adeptus, 'having attained'. Alchemists used it of anyone who had cracked the secret of gold.

definition: Administrative work; the paperwork side of things.
note: A clipping of administration. On the internet it also names whoever runs a forum or server.
hints: The person who can ban you from a server.

definition: To confess; or to let someone in.
note: From Latin admittere, 'to send to'. A ticket admits you; a guilty person admits fault.
hints: What a ticket does at the door.

definition: Sun-dried brick made of clay and straw.
note: From Spanish, via Arabic, from a Coptic word for brick, which goes back to ancient Egyptian. Few English words are older.
hints: Common building material in the American Southwest.
Mud brick dried in the sun.

definition: To take on as your own.
note: From Latin adoptare, 'to choose for oneself', from optare 'to choose'.
hints: Parents may do this with a child.
You can also do it with an idea.

definition: To love and admire deeply.
note: From Latin adorare, 'to speak to', meaning to pray. It was a word for worship before it was a word for fondness.

definition: To decorate or make beautiful.
note: From Latin adornare, 'to furnish', the same root as ornate and ornament.
hints: What jewellery does to a person.

definition: A fully grown person or animal.
note: From Latin adultus, 'grown up'. Adolescent comes from the same verb: one is growing, the other has grown.

definition: To attach; or a prefix or suffix.
note: From Latin affixus, 'fastened to'. Grammar borrowed it for the bits fastened onto words.
hints: To stick one thing to another.

definition: On fire.
note: Simply a- 'on' plus fire, like ablaze. It is used about passions as often as buildings.
hints: A heart might be described this way.

definition: Happening or being planned.
note: Literally 'on foot'. Sherlock Holmes made 'the game is afoot' famous, borrowing it from Shakespeare.
hints: Holmes says the game is this.

definition: In conflict with; in trouble with.
note: From a- plus foul. Ships ran afoul of each other when their rigging tangled.

definition: Later than; following.
note: From Old English æfter. 'Aftermath' first meant a second crop of grass mown after the first.

definition: Once more.
note: From Old English ongean, 'back'. 'Against' grew from the same word.

definition: With the mouth wide open in wonder.
note: A- plus gape. Its first known use is in Milton's Paradise Lost, in 1667.

definition: A banded, semi-precious stone.
note: From Greek achates, named after the river in Sicily where the stone was found.
hints: Marbles were once made of it.

definition: Someone who acts on another's behalf.
note: From Latin agens, 'doing'. A secret agent and a chemical agent both make things happen.
hints: Spies and estate brokers are both called this.

definition: Able to move quickly and easily.
note: From Latin agilis, 'nimble', from agere 'to drive'. Software teams adopted it in 2001.

definition: Glowing with light, warmth or happiness.
note: A- plus glow, like afire and ablaze. Faces are aglow as often as fires.
hints: A happy face might be this.

definition: Extreme physical or mental pain.
note: From Greek agonia, 'struggle', from agon, an athletic contest. The pain came from the effort.
hints: Its Greek root meant a contest.

definition: A public square or market in ancient Greece.
note: Greek for 'gathering place'. Agoraphobia is a fear of open, public spaces.
hints: Hidden in a word for fearing crowds.

definition: To share an opinion.
note: From Old French a gré, 'to one's liking', from Latin gratum, 'pleasing'.
hints: What two people do when they see eye to eye.

definition: In front; in the future.
note: A- plus head, probably first a sailor's word for beyond the ship's bow.

definition: A passage between rows of seats or shelves.
note: From Old French ele, 'wing', from Latin ala. It meant the side wings of a church before it meant a walkway.

definition: A warning of danger, or the device that sounds it.
note: From Italian all'arme, 'to arms!', the cry raised when an enemy appeared.
hints: It wakes you in the morning.
Once a call to grab weapons.

definition: A collection of recordings, or a book for photos.
note: Latin for a blank white tablet, from albus 'white'. Romans posted public notices on one.

definition: Watchful and ready.
note: From Italian all'erta, 'on the lookout', from erta, a high lookout post.

definition: Simple water plants such as seaweed and pond scum.
note: Plural of Latin alga, 'seaweed'. They produce much of the oxygen in the air.

definition: A being from another world; or anything foreign.
note: From Latin alienus, 'belonging to another', from alius, 'other'.
hints: Science fiction is full of them.

definition: To bring into a line.
note: From French aligner, from Latin linea, 'line'. Text, wheels and stars can all be aligned.
hints: What you do with text in a document.

definition: Similar; in the same way.
note: From Old English gelic, 'similar', related to the word like.

definition: Living; not dead.
note: From Old English on life, literally 'in life'. The a- in many such words is a worn-down 'on'.
hints: Full of energy, or simply breathing.

definition: To calm or lessen a fear or worry.
note: From Old English alecgan, 'to lay down'. You lay a fear to rest.
hints: To put a worry to rest.

definition: A narrow passage between buildings.
note: From Old French alee, 'a going', from aller 'to go'. A bowling alley is a long narrow lane too.
hints: Cats and bins live in one.

definition: To give out as a share.
note: From Old French aloter, 'to divide by lot'. Shares were once settled by drawing lots.
hints: What you do with time or seats.

definition: To let something happen.
note: From Old French alouer, which blended two Latin verbs, one for praise and one for placing.
hints: Parents decide what to do this with.

definition: A metal made by mixing two or more metals.
note: From Old French aloi, from a Latin word for binding together. Bronze is copper and tin.

definition: Up in the air.
note: From Old Norse a lopti, 'in the sky'. Sailors used it for anything up the mast.
hints: Up in the rigging, to a sailor.

definition: By yourself.
note: From all plus one, 'wholly one'. 'Lonely' was later formed from it by dropping the a-.

definition: Moving in a line beside something.
note: From Old English andlang, 'extending opposite'. You walk along a beach.

definition: Distant and cool towards others.
note: A sailing term: to keep a ship's head 'a loof', to windward, away from the shore.
hints: Its root is a sailing command.

definition: In a voice others can hear.
note: Simply a- plus loud. Reading aloud was normal; silent reading once astonished people.
hints: How you read to a child.

definition: The first letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Phoenician aleph, 'ox', whose letter was drawn as an ox head. Turn our A upside down and you can still see the horns.

definition: A table used for religious offerings or ceremonies.
note: From Latin altare, likely related to altus, 'high'. Weddings take place in front of one.
hints: Couples stand before one to marry.
A raised table in a church.

definition: To change.
note: From Latin alter, 'the other'. Altering something makes it other than it was.

definition: To gather a large amount.
note: From French amasser, 'to heap up', from masse, 'mass'.

definition: To astonish.
note: Middle English amasen meant to bewilder. 'Maze' is the same word: a place made to bewilder you.
hints: Related to a puzzle of paths.

definition: Fossilised tree resin, or its golden-orange colour.
note: From Arabic anbar, which first meant ambergris from whales. The name slid onto the resin.
hints: Insects are found trapped in it.

definition: To walk slowly and easily.
note: From Old French ambler, 'to walk like a horse', from Latin ambulare 'to walk'.

definition: To change to make better.
note: From Latin emendare, 'to remove a fault'. The US Constitution has twenty-seven of them.

definition: Wrong or out of place.
note: A- plus miss. 'Something is amiss' means something has missed its mark.

definition: Friendly relations.
note: From Old French amistie, from Latin amicus, 'friend'.

definition: Surrounded by; in the company of.
note: From Old English on gemang, 'in a crowd'.
hints: In the middle of a group.

definition: More than enough.
note: From Latin amplus, 'large, spacious'. Amplify comes from the same root.

definition: In a way that is more than enough.
note: From ample, from Latin amplus, 'large'. To be amply rewarded is to get plenty.
hints: How a debt might be repaid.

definition: To make someone laugh or smile.
note: From Old French amuser, 'to divert attention'. It first meant to fool or distract someone.
hints: What a clown tries to do.
Its old meaning was to distract.

definition: A heavenly messenger.
note: From Greek angelos, 'messenger'. Angels were defined by their job, carrying word from God.

definition: A strong feeling of displeasure.
note: From Old Norse angr, 'grief'. It meant sorrow before it meant rage.

definition: The space between two lines that meet.
note: From Latin angulus, 'corner'. Angling for fish comes from a different word meaning hook.

definition: Feeling or showing anger.
note: From anger, which in Old Norse meant grief or trouble.

definition: Japanese animated film and television.
note: A Japanese clipping of the English 'animation'. English borrowed the clipped word back.

definition: The joint between the foot and the leg.
note: From Old English ancleow. The bones were once compared to an angle or bend.

definition: An extra building attached to a main one; or to take over territory.
note: From Latin annexus, 'joined to'. Countries annex land; hotels have annexes.

definition: To irritate.
note: From Old French anoier, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred'. Ennui shares the root.

definition: To declare legally invalid.
note: From Latin annullare, 'to make nothing', from nullus.
hints: What can happen to a marriage.

definition: The positive electrode of a battery or cell.
note: Coined in 1834 for Michael Faraday, from Greek ana 'up' and hodos 'way'.

definition: Playful and silly behaviour.
note: From Italian antico, 'ancient', used for the strange creatures painted on Roman walls.
hints: Grotesque old paintings gave it its name.

definition: A heavy iron block on which metal is hammered.
note: From Old English anfilt, 'something beaten on'. One of the ear's tiny bones is named after it.

definition: The main artery leaving the heart.
note: From Greek aorte, 'that which is hung up'. Aristotle named it.
hints: Carries blood away from the heart.

definition: Separated by distance.
note: From French a part, 'to the side'.

definition: A small sap-sucking insect.
note: Linnaeus coined aphis in 1758, possibly misreading the Greek word for bug.

definition: A temporary pause in breathing, often during sleep.
note: From Greek apnoia, 'without breath'.

definition: A round fruit with crisp flesh.
note: Old English æppel meant any fruit. The fruit in Eden is never named as an apple.

definition: To put on; or to request formally.
note: From Latin applicare, 'to fold onto'. You apply paint, and apply for a job.
hints: You do it for a job.

definition: A garment worn over clothes to keep them clean.
note: Originally 'a napron'. People heard 'an apron', and the n moved across. Napkin keeps it.
hints: It lost its first letter to 'an'.

definition: In a fitting way.
note: From apt, from Latin aptus, 'fitted'.

definition: A shady garden shelter covered in climbing plants.
note: From Old French erbier, 'herb garden'. People later linked it to Latin arbor, 'tree'.

definition: An enclosed area for sport or shows.
note: Latin for 'sand'. Roman arenas were strewn with it to soak up the blood.

definition: To disagree with words.
note: From Latin arguere, 'to make clear'. It was once about proving a point, not fighting.

definition: To come into being; to get up.
note: From Old English arisan, 'to rise'.
hints: To stand up, in older English.

definition: Protective covering worn in battle.
note: From Latin armatura, 'equipment', from arma, 'weapons'.

definition: A distinctive, usually pleasant smell.
note: From Greek aroma, 'spice'. In Latin it was used in the plural for spices and sweet herbs.
hints: Coffee and fresh bread have one.

definition: An impressive range or display of things.
note: From Old French areer, 'to put in order'. Programmers use it for an ordered list of values.
hints: A list of values, to a programmer.

definition: A pointed shaft shot from a bow.
note: From Old English earh. Its shape now points the way on every sign and screen.

definition: The crime of deliberately setting fire to property.
note: From Old French arsoun, from Latin ardere, 'to burn'. Ardent shares the root.

definition: Showily artistic or bohemian.
note: An American form of arty, from arts plus -y. Often said with a slight eye-roll.

definition: A wide silk tie looped under the chin.
note: Named after Royal Ascot, the racecourse where fashionable men wore them.

definition: Pale grey, especially from shock or illness.
note: From ash plus -en, 'made of ash'. Faces turn ashen with fright.
hints: The colour of something burnt out.

definition: To one side; or a remark made quietly.
note: From Old English on side. In theatre, an aside is spoken to the audience, unheard by the others on stage.
hints: Actors speak one to the audience.

definition: Not straight; crooked.
note: A- plus skew. A picture on a wall can hang this way.

definition: A test of a metal's purity.
note: From Old French assai, 'trial'. Essay comes from the same word: an essay is an attempt.

definition: A ring-shaped coral island around a lagoon.
note: From Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives, where the country is made of them.
hints: The Maldives are built of them.

definition: To make amends for a wrong.
note: From 'at one'. To atone was to bring two sides into harmony again.

definition: The space just below a roof.
note: From Attica, the region around Athens: its architectural style used a decorated top storey.
hints: Old boxes are stored up there.
Named after the region around Athens.

definition: An official check of accounts.
note: From Latin auditus, 'hearing'. Accounts were once read aloud to the examiner.

definition: To be a sign of what will happen.
note: A Roman augur foretold the future from the flight of birds. Inauguration began with one.
hints: Things may bode well or ill this way.
Romans read birds to do it.

definition: An aunt, or an affectionate name for an older woman.
note: A pet form of aunt. In many cultures it is used for any respected older woman.
hints: A fond name for an older woman.

definition: Use or benefit.
note: From Old French valoir, 'to be worth'. 'To no avail' means it did no good.

definition: To turn away; to prevent.
note: From Latin avertere, 'to turn from'. You avert your eyes, or a disaster.
hints: What you do with your eyes from a horror.

definition: Relating to birds.
note: From Latin avis, 'bird'. Aviation comes from the same root.
hints: Bird flu is this kind of influenza.

definition: To stay away from.
note: From Old French esvuidier, 'to empty out'. Void shares the root.
hints: What you do with an ex in the street.

definition: To wait for.
note: From Old French awaitier, 'to lie in wait'.

definition: Not asleep.
note: From Old English awacan, 'to arise'. Two older verbs, one for waking up and one for being up, merged into it.

definition: A prize given for achievement.
note: From Old French awarder, 'to observe, then decide'. It began as a judge's decision.

definition: Knowing about something.
note: From Old English gewær, 'watchful'. Wary shares the root.

definition: Flooded or covered with water.
note: A- plus wash. A rock is awash when waves just cover it.
hints: A city might be this with tourists.

definition: Very bad.
note: Awe plus -ful. It once meant full of awe, inspiring wonder, before it slid to dreadful.

definition: Relating to an axis.
note: From Latin axis, 'axle'. An axial line runs down the centre of something.

definition: A statement accepted as true without proof.
note: From Greek axioma, 'what is thought worthy'. Euclid's geometry is built on five.

definition: A proposed subatomic particle.
note: Coined by physicist Frank Wilczek in 1978, who named it after a brand of laundry detergent because it 'cleaned up' a problem.

definition: Bright blue, like a clear sky.
note: From Arabic lazaward, 'lapis lazuli', the blue stone. The first letter fell off in Old French.
hints: The colour of a cloudless sky.

definition: Cured meat from the back and sides of a pig.
note: From Old French bacon, 'back meat'. Bringing home the bacon first meant winning a prize.

definition: A small sign worn to show identity or achievement.
note: Of uncertain origin; first used for heraldic symbols showing whose household you served.

definition: In a poor or unsatisfactory way.
note: Bad plus -ly. To want something badly is to want it very much.
hints: How you want something you crave.

definition: A ring-shaped bread roll, boiled then baked.
note: From Yiddish beygl, from a German word for ring or bracelet.
hints: A bread roll with a hole.

definition: Loose and hanging away from the body.
note: Bag plus -y. Baggy jeans had a revival in the nineties and again in the 2020s.

definition: Someone who makes bread and cakes.
note: From Old English bæcere. A baker's dozen is thirteen, an extra loaf against short weight.

definition: A machine that packs hay or straw into bales.
note: From bale, a bundle. Farmers tow them behind tractors.

definition: Pleasantly warm.
note: From balm, a soothing ointment. A balmy evening soothes like one.

definition: Boring and unoriginal.
note: From Old French ban, 'compulsory feudal service'. Shared by everyone, so commonplace.
hints: Common to the point of boredom.

definition: A stringed instrument with a round drum-like body.
note: Brought to America by enslaved West Africans, from an instrument like the akonting.

definition: A flat-bottomed boat for carrying goods on rivers.
note: From Old French barge, via Latin barca, 'small boat'. To barge in is to push in clumsily.
hints: To push rudely into a room.

definition: A nobleman of the lowest rank; or a powerful businessman.
note: From Old French barun, 'man, warrior'. Robber barons were the ruthless tycoons of the 1800s.
hints: Media or oil tycoons are called this.

definition: Forming the base; fundamental.
note: From base. Your basal metabolic rate is what your body burns at rest.

definition: An aromatic herb used in cooking.
note: From Greek basilikon, 'royal'. It was considered a herb fit for kings.

definition: A bowl for washing, or a large dip in land.
note: From Old French bacin, from Latin baccinum, 'water vessel'.

definition: The foundation or starting point for something.
note: From Greek basis, 'step' or 'pedestal'. Base shares the root.
hints: Facts form this for an argument.

definition: A quantity made at one time.
note: From Old English, 'something baked'. A batch was first the bread from a single firing.
hints: Cookies come out of the oven in one.

definition: To wash in water, or swim.
note: From Old English baþian. Sunbathing borrowed it for lying in light.
hints: Sunlight can do it to a room.

definition: A short stick used by a conductor, relay runner or officer.
note: From French bâton, 'stick'. Passing the baton means handing over responsibility.

definition: Slightly mad.
note: From 'bats in the belfry', for a head full of fluttering thoughts.
